title: Sparse KV & Probing Scrapbook — Quincy Wells
content:
Purpose:
Quick personal notebook: collect short summaries of papers/blog posts about sparse/partitioned KV memory, probing techniques for long-context behavior, and a running list of experiments I want to try on our infra (Dedicated + local sim). This is deliberately informal — scraps, commands, TODOs, and questions to bring into a short spike.

Quick framing: why I care
- Production inference needs: long effective context without linear cost growth; avoid catastrophic slowdown / OOMs when KV grows.
- Sparse/partitioned KV (sharding, inverted-index lookups, lightweight retrieval of cached KV) could give good latency/cost tradeoffs for long sessions.
- Probing methods help measure how much model uses retrieved KV vs recency priors. Need practical evals not just synthetic prompts.

Papers / posts skimmed (notes + one-line takeaway)
1) "Sparse KV: Indexing and Routing for Long Context" (arXiv 2025) — main idea: build a small index over KV keys (hashed embeddings + PQ), route attention to relevant shards.
   - takeaway: index + top-k shard selection reduces per-token compute by ~2-6x for long contexts in eval. Accuracy drop minimal when shard selection recall > 0.9.
   - practical: need fast approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) that works with GPU KV format; CPU-based FAISS introduces host-GPU transfer overheads.

2) "KV Eviction Policies at Scale" (conference talk, June 2025) — compares LRU variants, recency+semantic hybrid, and TTL-based culling for chat sessions.
   - takeaway: simple TTL+semantic score (similarity to recent prompt embeddings) beats pure LRU for long multi-turn dialogs. Eviction is critical to bound mem while keeping quality.

3) "Probing Long-Context Use with Synthetic Inserts" (workshop paper) — inserts sentinel facts and measures recall over time and distractors.
   - takeaway: models often reconstruct inserted facts even when KV omitted, i.e., strong recency-induced hallucination; probing needs adversarial distractors to be informative.

4) Engineering blog posts: "Building a Sharded KV Cache for Inference" (teamX blog).
   - takeaway: implementation gotchas: alignment of KV layout to attention kernel expectations, tokenization drift, and boundary conditions when switching shards mid-generation.

Notes from reading / immediate ideas
- Index placement: keep lightweight index on host + compact embeddings on GPU so selection is host-side cheap but data stays local for selected shards. But that implies careful batching to avoid PCIe thrash.
- Approximate recall target: aim for 0.95 recall at Kshards=8 for stable generation quality. Measure with holdout prompts.
- Eviction heuristic to try: hybrid TTL (per-session base) + semantic score = dot(query, key) over last-turn embedding; downweight old keys gradually.
- Quantization: 8-bit keys fine, but values (KV vectors for past activations) need to be 16-bit or 8-bit with calibrated scale — test quant noise on completions.

Planned experiments (ordered short spike -> medium -> long)
- Spike A (2 days): replay a single-session workload (1000 chat sessions) through local sim using our serving runtime but replaced KV store with a naive host-side ANN (nmslib). Measure: median latency per token, 95p latency, throughput, and token-level fidelity (BLEU-ish sketch).
   commands / pseudo: 
   - run_sim --model gpt-7b --kv-backend naive-ann --shards 16 --session-set sessions/sample-1000.json --trace out/spikeA.json
   - extract_metrics.py out/spikeA.json --metrics lat95,lat50,tokens-per-sec,recall@k

- Spike B (3 days): TTL+semantic eviction: roll forward spike A but with hybrid eviction policy; measure memory footprint over time and quality on 200 long sessions (>4k tokens).

- Medium (1 week): Implement host-index + GPU pinned shards: profile PCIe copies, add small prefetch window to hide transfer. Key metric: additional latency introduced by selection vs saved attention compute.

- Long (2+ weeks): Production-like A/B on Dedicated pool with canary: compare default continuous KV (no sharding) vs shard+index with fallback when index misses. Watch for tail-latency regressions and failure modes (stale shards).

Evaluation heuristics to implement quickly
- 'sentinel recall' test: insert synthetic named facts into session, then later probe with multiple paraphrases. Measure precision@N and response score via heuristics.
- output divergence measure: compute LM-logprob gap between using full KV vs sharded-kv; large gap indicates heavy dependence on pruned context.
- human-lite rubric: ask raters (or use proxy metric with a smaller instruction-tuned eval model) to check whether essential facts are preserved.

Open questions / unknowns
- What is the best representation for keys? token-level position + embedding? Or span-level summary vector? Tradeoffs: smaller keys -> cheaper index but lower recall.
- Can we do dynamic K selection per layer? (early layers access fewer shards, later layers more refined selection) Complexity high but potentially big wins.
- How to handle cross-session shared keys (global cache) vs per-session ephemeral keys — blend policy?

Rough notes / snippets
- On selection batching: group queries by model batch then combine ANN requests into a single batched query to index to reduce host-call overhead. Cache index results for repeated queries across tokens in same generation step.
- When index misses, fallback to fallback-model-variant: lower-cost model that still has good long-memory (e.g., larger KV compression). Make sure our rollout system (console) can toggle fallback quickly.

Todo (short):
- [ ] implement synthetic sentinel generator (scripts/sentinel_gen.py)
- [ ] add recall@k measurement to existing eval harness (eval/kv_recall.py)
- [ ] wire hybrid TTL-semantic eviction into local sim (kv_store/eviction.py)
- [ ] spike host-index selection and log PCIe copy times

Meeting notes to bring to sync with Mika / Arun:
- Quick plan: 1) run Spike A by EOD Fri; 2) if recall drop >5% at target shards, try increasing Kfirst; 3) instrument per-token kernel time to find bottleneck.
- Risks to flag: potential for increased tail latency; complexity of debugging model-quality regressions when KV is partial.

Random brain dump (low priority):
- Could try "progressive reveal" where we only attach a small window of most relevant KV to the attention context but keep a compressed summary in model tokens (prompt-level index). Might reduce fetch overhead but costs prompt tokens.
